lessons.title: Signals: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL
lessons.goal:
Learn what a signal is, the difference between asking a process to stop (SIGTERM) and forcing it (SIGKILL), and how to read the exit codes.

Why it matters: `kill -9` as a first reaction skips the program's cleanup (flushing files, removing locks). The right order is TERM first, KILL only if needed.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. Scripts and C programs are saved there.

steps.title: A signal is a small message to a process
steps.text: A **signal** is a number the kernel delivers to a process. The process can run a handler, ignore it, or the kernel applies a default action (terminate, stop, ignore). `kill -l` lists them.

run.output:
1) SIGHUP	 2) SIGINT	 3) SIGQUIT	 4) SIGILL	 5) SIGTRAP
 6) SIGABRT	 7) SIGBUS	 8) SIGFPE	 9) SIGKILL	10) SIGUSR1
11) SIGSEGV	12) SIGUSR2	13) SIGPIPE	14) SIGALRM	15) SIGTERM
16) SIGSTKFLT	17) SIGCHLD	18) SIGCONT	19) SIGSTOP	20) SIGTSTP

steps.title: kill sends a signal
steps.text: Despite the name, `kill` just sends a signal. The default is SIGTERM (15). A process killed by signal N ends with exit status 128+N. We start a sleeper, send TERM, and read the status.

run.cmd: sleep 100 & p=$!; kill -TERM $p; wait $p; echo "exit status: $?"
sleep 100 & p=$!; kill -KILL $p; wait $p; echo "exit status: $?"
sleep 100 & p=$!; kill -INT $p; wait $p; echo "exit status: $?"

steps.title: SIGTERM can be handled
steps.text: A program can catch SIGTERM and clean up. This script traps TERM and INT. `exit 0` after cleanup ends it normally.

code.src:
#!/bin/bash
trap 'echo "got SIGTERM, cleaning up"; exit 0' TERM
trap 'echo "got SIGINT, ignoring it"' INT
echo "worker started"
while true; do sleep 0.2; done

run.cmd: chmod +x worker.sh; ./worker.sh > worker.out & p=$!; sleep 1; kill -INT $p; kill -TERM $p; wait $p; echo "exit status: $?"; cat worker.out
run.output:
[1] 3463546
exit status: 0
worker started
got SIGTERM, cleaning up

steps.title: SIGKILL cannot be handled
steps.text: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP go straight to the kernel. The process gets no chance to run code. No `trap` can catch them. The program leaves no clean exit: temporary files and locks stay behind.

run.cmd: ./worker.sh > worker.out & p=$!; sleep 1; kill -KILL $p; wait $p; echo "exit status: $?"; cat worker.out

steps.under: When a signal is sent, the kernel sets a bit in the target's pending-signal set. At the next return to user mode the kernel checks it: for a caught signal it builds a frame on the user stack and runs the handler; for SIGKILL it just tears the process down. This is why a process in `D` state does not die until it returns from kernel mode.

steps.title: Which one first?
steps.text: Standard practice: send SIGTERM, wait a few seconds, and only then SIGKILL. `systemd` does exactly this when it stops a service (`TimeoutStopSec`, then SIGKILL).

run.cmd: sleep 100 & p=$!; kill $p; sleep 0.2; kill -0 $p 2>/dev/null && echo alive || echo "gone after TERM"

steps.after: `kill -0 PID` sends no signal; it only tests whether the process exists and you may signal it.

quiz.q: Which signal cannot be caught or ignored?
A process dies from SIGTERM. What exit status does the shell report?

options: The program can clean up (close files, remove locks) on SIGTERM
quiz.explain: SIGKILL gives the program no chance to clean up.

options: Checks whether PID exists and can be signalled
quiz.explain: No signal is sent; only the check is done.

check.scenario: A service ignores `kill PID` and keeps running. Describe your next steps in order.
check.answer:
1. Check the state with `ps -o stat,wchan -p PID`. If it is `D`, signals wait; find the I/O cause.
2. If it is `S`/`R`, the program may ignore or block SIGTERM (`grep Sig /proc/PID/status`).
3. Wait a short time, then `kill -KILL PID`. Afterwards remove stale locks/PID files and check for orphaned children.

lessons.title: SIGHUP, SIGCHLD, trap and nohup
lessons.goal:
Learn the signals daemons use every day: SIGHUP (reload), SIGCHLD (a child ended), SIGUSR1/2, and how shell `trap` and `nohup` use them.

Why it matters: `systemctl reload` sends SIGHUP to many services. Scripts need `trap` to clean up their temporary files.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. Scripts and C programs are saved there.

steps.title: SIGHUP means "reload your configuration"
steps.text: Historically SIGHUP meant the terminal hung up. Daemons have no terminal, so many reuse it as "re-read your config". This script loads a message from a file and reloads it on SIGHUP, without restarting.

run.cmd: echo first > /tmp/lab/msg.conf; chmod +x reloader.sh; ./reloader.sh > reload.out & p=$!; sleep 1; echo second > /tmp/lab/msg.conf; kill -HUP $p; sleep 1; kill $p; wait $p 2>/dev/null; cat reload.out
run.output:
[1] 3463573
config is: first
SIGHUP: reloading
config is: second

steps.title: SIGCHLD tells a parent that a child ended
steps.text: The kernel sends **SIGCHLD** to the parent when a child exits or stops. Programs use it to call `wait`. In bash, `trap ... CHLD` shows it.

run.cmd: bash -c 'trap "echo SIGCHLD received" CHLD; sleep 1 & wait; echo parent done'

steps.title: trap runs code on a signal, and on exit
steps.text: `trap 'CMD' SIGNAL` runs CMD when the shell receives the signal. The pseudo-signal `EXIT` runs when the script ends for any reason, which makes it the right place to delete temporary files.

run.cmd: bash -c 't=$(mktemp); trap "rm -f $t; echo cleaned $(basename $t | cut -c1-3)" EXIT; echo work > $t; echo working; exit 3'; echo "script status: $?"

steps.title: nohup ignores SIGHUP
steps.text: `nohup CMD` starts CMD with SIGHUP ignored and output sent to `nohup.out`. The ignored-signal mask is inherited, so children also ignore it. We compare a plain and a nohup process; bit 1 of `SigIgn` is SIGHUP.

run.cmd: sleep 100 & a=$!; nohup sleep 100 > /dev/null 2>&1 & b=$!; sleep 0.3; kill -HUP $a $b; sleep 0.3; ps -o pid= -p $a > /dev/null && echo "plain: alive" || echo "plain: killed by SIGHUP"; ps -o pid= -p $b > /dev/null && echo "nohup: alive" || echo "nohup: killed"; kill $b
run.output:
[1] 3463602
[2] 3463603
plain: killed by SIGHUP
nohup: alive

steps.title: Signals for you to define
steps.text: SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 have no fixed meaning. Programs use them for custom actions: dump statistics, rotate logs, toggle debug output.

run.cmd: bash -c 'trap "echo got USR1: dumping stats" USR1; kill -USR1 $$; echo after'

steps.under: `dd` prints its progress on SIGUSR1, `nginx` reopens its log files on SIGUSR1 (used by logrotate), and `unicorn`/`gunicorn` use TTIN/TTOU to change the worker count.

quiz.q: What do most daemons do on SIGHUP?
quiz.explain: It is a convention for "re-read your config".

quiz.q: Which trap runs when a bash script ends for any reason?
quiz.explain: EXIT runs at every exit; ideal for cleanup.

quiz.q: When does a parent receive SIGCHLD?
options: When a child exits or stops
quiz.explain: That is how it learns it should call wait.

quiz.q: Which tool makes a command ignore SIGHUP?
quiz.explain: nohup sets SIGHUP to ignored before exec.

check.scenario: Logrotate renamed `app.log` but the application keeps writing to the renamed file. What do you configure so the app opens a new file?
check.answer: Send the signal the app uses for "reopen logs" in a `postrotate` script (often `kill -HUP $(cat /run/app.pid)` or `systemctl reload app`), or use `copytruncate` as a last resort. The reason: the app holds the old file open by descriptor; only a reopen makes it write to the new name.

lessons.title: Signal delivery underneath: masks, pending, coalescing
lessons.goal:
See how the kernel stores signals: a blocked mask, a pending set and a handler table, and why several identical signals can merge into one.

Why it matters: it explains lost signals ("I sent 3 SIGUSR1 and the handler ran once"), and why you must write handlers that only set a flag.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. Scripts and C programs are saved there.

steps.title: A test program
steps.text: The program installs a handler for SIGUSR1, **blocks** SIGUSR1, sends itself three, prints the kernel's mask fields, then unblocks. It also tries to install a handler for SIGKILL.

run.output:
sigaction(SIGKILL): Invalid argument
SigPnd:	0000000000000200
SigBlk:	0000000000010200
SigCgt:	0000000000000200
handler ran 1 time(s) after 3 signals

steps.title: Read the three fields
steps.text:
`SigBlk` is the blocked mask, `SigPnd` the pending mask, `SigCgt` the caught mask. Each is a bit set: bit N-1 is signal N. SIGUSR1 is signal 10, so its bit is `0x200`.

The handler ran **once** for three signals. (`SigBlk` also shows bit `0x10000`: signal 17, SIGCHLD, which `system()` blocks while it runs the `grep`.) Standard signals are not queued: while one is pending, further identical signals are merged.

steps.title: The state of a live process
steps.text: The same fields exist for any process. A shell waiting for input has no signals pending and a few caught.
steps.under: Each task has a `blocked` mask, a `pending` set and a table of `sigaction` structs. `kill()` sets the bit in `pending` (if not ignored) and wakes the task. On return to user mode the kernel looks at `pending & ~blocked` and delivers. Real-time signals (SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX) **are** queued with data (`sigqueue`), standard signals are not.

steps.title: Why handlers must be tiny
steps.text: A handler can interrupt the program at any instruction, even in the middle of `malloc` or `printf`. Only **async-signal-safe** functions are allowed. The usual pattern: the handler sets a flag (`volatile sig_atomic_t`), and the main loop checks it. This is what `hits++` does in the demo.

quiz.q: You send SIGUSR1 five times quickly to a process that has it blocked. How many handler runs after unblocking?
quiz.explain: Standard signals are coalesced while pending.

quiz.q: Which field of /proc/PID/status shows signals waiting for delivery?

options: SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored

quiz.q: What should a signal handler do?
options: Almost nothing: set a flag and return

check.scenario: A daemon sometimes misses a SIGUSR1 sent by a monitoring script in a burst of three. How do you make this robust?
check.answer: Do not use counts of signals as protocol. Use one signal as "wake up and look" and let the program read a file or queue to learn what to do. If you need every event, use real-time signals (`sigqueue`), a pipe or a socket, which queue data.

interview.q: What is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
interview.a: SIGTERM asks the process to terminate and can be caught for cleanup. SIGKILL is enforced by the kernel and cannot be caught or ignored. See [the lesson](#/lesson/11/sigterm-sigkill).

interview.q: What exit status does a process killed by SIGKILL have?
What is SIGHUP used for today?
interview.a: Originally terminal hang-up. Now most daemons reload their configuration on it. nohup makes a command ignore it. See [the lesson](#/lesson/11/sighup-sigchld-trap).

interview.q: How do you clean up temporary files in a shell script reliably?
interview.a: `trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT`. EXIT runs on normal exit, on `exit`, and (with TERM/INT trapped to exit) on signals. It does not run on SIGKILL.
Yes. Standard signals are not queued: identical pending signals merge. See [the lesson](#/lesson/11/signals-underneath). Use real-time signals or another channel when counts matter.

interview.q: Why does kill -9 on a D-state process not work?
interview.a: The signal stays pending until the process returns from the uninterruptible kernel wait, so it is delivered only afterwards.

glossary.def: A numbered notification the kernel delivers to a process.
Signal 15: polite request to terminate; can be caught.
Signal 9: forced termination, cannot be caught or ignored.
Signal 1: hangup; many daemons reload configuration on it.
Signal sent to a parent when a child exits or stops.
A bash builtin that runs a command when a signal or EXIT occurs.
The set of signals a process currently blocks.
A signal that was sent but not yet delivered, for example because it is blocked.

commands.desc: Run cleanup when the script ends.
Show blocked, pending, ignored, caught masks.
